props.title: The Filth and the Fury
props.initialSlug: Sex Pistols documentary capturing punk's first wave

sections.content: Julien Temple's raw, revolutionary documentary The Filth and the Fury redefines punk history through the chaotic lens of the Sex Pistols. Unlike Temple's earlier The Great Rock 'n' Roll Swindle (1980), this film gives voice to the actual band members, particularly Johnny Rotten/John Lydon, whose razor-sharp wit and unfiltered honesty cut through decades of mythology. The film masterfully weaves archival footage with contemporary interviews, showing band members in silhouette - a technique later echoed in Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck (2015).

sections.content: Temple's documentary technique revolutionized music filmmaking, influencing works like Joe Strummer: The Future Is Unwritten (2007) and What We Do Is Secret (2007). The film's greatest triumph is contextualizing the Pistols within Britain's social collapse of the 1970s, using clips from British television shows and news reports to paint a picture of a nation in decay. This approach influenced later docs like Amy (2015) and Oasis: Supersonic (2016).

The film's unflinching look at Sid Vicious's decline and death marks a stark contrast to earlier punk documentaries like D.O.A.: A Right of Passage (1980) and The Decline of Western Civilization (1981). Temple's access to intimate footage and the band's willingness to finally tell their story honestly creates a documentary that's both historical record and emotional confession. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Punk Documentary

movies.title: Control
movies.slug: Anton Corbijn's haunting biopic of Joy Division's Ian Curtis

sections.content: Temple's approach influenced a new wave of punk documentaries that prioritized authenticity over mythology. Films like American Hardcore (2006) and Bad Brains: A Band in DC (2012) followed Temple's lead in examining the social conditions that birthed their subjects. The Filth and the Fury's impact can be seen in recent works like L7: Pretend We're Dead (2016) and Bad Reputation (2018), which similarly balance archival footage with candid reflection.
